Its buggy.... like.. infuriatingly buggy.... It could be a great game, but the number of times ive been stuck under rocks after 25 minutes of climbing just for it to kill me and send me to the bottom is embarrassing from a coding stand point. Once you get to zone 4 and the stamina depletion bubbles hit you, you can guarantee itll possess your corpse to the edge of the zone where youll be guaranteed to be sent to the bottom. Make it make a little bit of sense, its fun climbing but having a single thing completely ♥♥♥♥ you with absolutely no way to recover is poor design.

Charming and comfy. The music really hits a good spot and the world is quite inviting. The controls are quite basic but allows to test ways of reaching tricky spots. When it wants to work as intended it feels quite enjoyable as you swing around and climb upwards to your goal just before the stamina runs out. One problem is its level-generation. At times it is giving you the right amount of challenge on reaching the goal and does give you some good "check-points" in the shape of hooks where you can regain. In other times it gives you a situation where you cannot climb over or around at all like covering the area with rock which cannot be grabbed. This ends the entire run, making the experience really sour when you aim to do the whole journey from start.

Cute, Charming, but in the End… Frustrating! The game starts strong with an engaging and fun gameplay experience that’s just the right amount of difficulty to keep you motivated to push forward. But as you move deeper into the game, especially when you hit World 2, the fun starts to fade. New mechanics come into play that seem to drain the joy right out of the experience. Instead of enjoying the climb, you find yourself battling the physics engine, with glitches galore that make you feel like you’re not in control. I’d understand if this was a “get good” game and I just needed to improve, but it’s not even about that. It’s more about the game itself losing its charm. What started as an engaging journey ends up feeling more like a test of patience than skill. My enjoyment eventually just… left. Maybe they can add some more patches and I will come back but for now it hits the shelf :(

I really want to love this game, and I did at first. It has a great atmosphere and sense of humour, and simply put it is just a fun game. I blasted through it, unable to put it down for the first few hours. It was challenging in a way that was enjoyable and encouraging. However, once you pass a certain threshold, the game becomes no longer challenging, but impossible. The procedural generation will 90% of the time give you an unsolvable course the further into the game you get. It's not even that it's hard or difficult, it's completely unfair. Mechanics will fail exactly when you need them; I couldn't tell you how many times one of the harness ropes randomly unclasped and left me at the start of the course, in a randomly generated pit with no way out, or just dead. Every so often I come back because I remember how fun it was at first, and then am quickly reminded that it's not a game of skill, growth, or perseverance, it's a game of chance. There are a bunch of other, smaller, bugs I've encountered, but I am BEGGING the devs to fix the procedural generation and harness mechanics.

ENG: Tried the demo and I fell in love with it, it has a nostalgic vibe that reminds me of games from another era, a charisma perhaps typical of classic Nintendo games or something, I don't know. Also, the mechanics are interesting, with the gamepad because it's clearly a game designed to be played with a controller. We can hold on to certain edges and surfaces with our hands, as well as rotate to gain momentum, double jump and use a variety of objects, all of which is very fun. Frustrating? Yes, but not to the degree of "Getting Over It". Most of the levels are individual and not so long that it hurts too much to restart them, and there are upgrades you can buy that help a lot. I haven't played for too long, but I'm really enjoying it and I wanted to say so. Listen, I wanted to like Surmount. It was highly recommended by a few content creators that are typically spot on, The art style and *theoretical* game play appealed to me. But my god, the bugs and inconsistent controls were a deal breaker. I tried the rotation to spin and the auto-spin - neither one was predictable enough to use properly. More often than not I would fling myself in the opposite direction. Three solid hours of playing tutorial levels, starter side missions, and the first few areas of the actual mountain. I could not for the life of me figure out the right time to let go to go in a desired direction. The second area with ice is where the bugs **really** kicked off. I would be hanging from a piton, look at my phone because of a notification, and when I turned back, I would be flung halfway across the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ map with my rope snapped and a ton of progress lost. But what made me uninstall the game was when I finished the campfire side mission in the second area - I just had to get back to the start of the level with suddenly all controls just stopped working. Wired controller - nothing. Keyboard - also nothing. Just... nothing.

Ledges are completely broken to the point where I'm surprised it was released in this state. Any section that requires using ledges to climb up are completely unplayable. The way this integral game mechanic is supposed to work is by allowing normal swings when grabbed below the ledge and near impossible momentum for swings above. The problem with this obstacle isn't even that the hitbox is insanely small below the ledge and gigantic above, since that can be chocked up to game difficultly. The problem is that the mechanic is a complete lie and ledges are impossible to swing on several hand lengths below the ledge. That, combined with the insanely small hitbox, means some ledges will just be impossible to progress from; and when they comprise a whole vertical section, it becomes impossible to continue the game. Now, it's possible everyone I've played the game with, including me, is bad or that pixel hunting for a spot to grab with a death timer counting down is actually good game design. But I wouldn't have spent money on it if I knew how little of the game would be playable.

incredibly fun on a mechanical level! the music's great, the climbing is really satisfying especially once you progress a bit and get some of the upgrades. it's a procedurally-generated, level-based layout, so there's quite a bit of replay value, and it's not too punishing if you fail and have to go back a bit. the big issue with the game is the bugs. i didn't initially notice any, the climbing itself is actually really polished, but the level generation can really freak out sometimes in ways that make the game hard to recommend on its own. one of my levels (3-2?) was always the same seed, one time a level generated completely empty, etc. it's super fun if you can get past the bugs, but given that there haven't been any updates basically since release, don't expect that to change anytime soon.

cant recommend while its still broken unfortunately. there is a risk of it generating a level that is impossible to clear, and for whatever reason there is no way of getting a newly generated level to beat instead. as far as the developer could tell the last time they looked into it, they didnt experience this problem, which is why i say "risk". it seems some players have to just be unlucky enough to play up to that point and get stuck forever. and the generated level must be tied to something cause it persisted between pc and steam deck. anyway outside of that its a great game, just unfortunate that it works that way.

Surmount: A Mountain Climbing Adventure is a delightful indie platforming experience developed by Jasper Oprel and Indiana-Jonas and published by Indiana-Jonas. Built around the simple concept of climbing a gigantic mountain, the game transforms that premise into a memorable adventure filled with physics-driven challenges, exploration, humor, and a surprising amount of personality. Rather than focusing on realism, Surmount embraces a playful approach that encourages experimentation and rewards persistence, making every climb feel like a unique story of success, failure, and discovery. The core gameplay revolves around ascending the massive Mount Om using a movement system based on physics and momentum. Players must grab ledges, swing across gaps, and carefully navigate increasingly complex terrain while dealing with the unpredictability that comes with the game's mechanics. This creates a constant sense of tension because every movement matters, yet the controls remain approachable enough for newcomers. Reaching a difficult ledge after several failed attempts feels genuinely rewarding, while unexpected slips and tumbles often lead to humorous situations instead of frustration. The mountain itself becomes both the game's setting and its greatest challenge, continuously testing the player's adaptability. One of the strongest aspects of Surmount is how it combines handcrafted design with procedural elements. As players progress higher, they encounter a wide variety of environments, obstacles, and surprises that prevent the adventure from becoming repetitive. Exploration is encouraged through hidden areas, optional routes, and encounters that reward curiosity. The mountain feels alive with opportunities to wander off the main path, making the journey to the summit as important as the destination itself. This sense of freedom helps create an experience that feels larger and more dynamic than its relatively straightforward premise might initially suggest. The game's narrative takes a lighthearted approach, introducing a cast of eccentric characters scattered throughout the mountain. These individuals provide amusing conversations, side activities, and bits of world-building that add charm to the adventure. The writing never takes itself too seriously, which fits perfectly with the game's colorful atmosphere. Instead of relying on dramatic storytelling, Surmount succeeds by creating a cheerful world filled with quirky personalities that make the climb more enjoyable and memorable. Visually, the game adopts a vibrant cartoon art style that complements its whimsical tone. The bright environments and expressive character designs help establish an inviting atmosphere from the very beginning. While the graphics are relatively simple, they are polished and full of character, giving each region of the mountain its own identity. The visual clarity also serves an important gameplay function, making it easier to read terrain and plan routes while climbing. Combined with a relaxing soundtrack, the presentation creates a pleasant and uplifting adventure that remains engaging throughout its duration. Another highlight is the cooperative mode, which allows two players to tackle the mountain together. The addition of a rope connecting both climbers creates opportunities for teamwork, coordination, and plenty of comedic mishaps. Cooperative play changes the dynamic considerably, as players must communicate and work together to overcome obstacles that might be simple in solo play. The result is an experience that can be equally rewarding and hilarious, making it a great option for friends looking for a cooperative challenge. Surmount also includes character customization, achievements, and additional objectives that provide extra motivation to continue exploring. These features help extend the game's longevity and give completionists more reasons to revisit different parts of the mountain. While the primary objective remains reaching the summit, the additional content ensures that players can enjoy the adventure at their own pace without feeling rushed toward the end. The game's main drawback is that its physics-based movement can occasionally feel inconsistent. There are moments when a seemingly simple maneuver goes wrong due to an awkward interaction with the environment, leading to an unexpected fall. Players seeking absolute precision may find these situations frustrating, especially during more difficult sections. However, much of the game's appeal comes from embracing this unpredictability, and many players will likely view these moments as part of the experience rather than a serious flaw. Overall, Surmount: A Mountain Climbing Adventure delivers a refreshing blend of exploration, platforming, and comedy. Its charming presentation, inventive mountain design, entertaining physics system, and enjoyable cooperative mode come together to create an adventure that stands out among indie platformers. The journey to the top is filled with memorable moments, and the game's emphasis on fun over frustration makes it accessible to a wide audience. While the occasional control inconsistency may cause minor setbacks, the overall experience remains highly enjoyable from beginning to end. Surmount succeeds in turning mountain climbing into a fun, creative, and surprisingly engaging adventure, offering plenty of charm, challenge, and replay value for players who enjoy exploration and physics-based platforming. Rating: 8/10
